Hypothesis: We hypothesize that in liver neoplasms, elevated levels of GEMIN5—augmented by concurrent deregulation of regulatory lncRNAs—directly modulate the splicing of key DNA repair genes, RAD51 and MRE11. This modulation results in the formation of alternative, noncanonical isoforms that compromise efficient high-fidelity homologous recombination and instead promote error-prone break-induced replication (BIR). The ensuing genomic instability drives enhanced metastatic and angiogenic potential, culminating in worsened clinical outcomes. To validate this, we will employ CRISPR/Cas9 editing to modulate GEMIN5 expression and use enhanced CLIP-seq to demonstrate its direct interaction with RAD51 and MRE11 transcripts. Complementary high-throughput isoform-specific RNA sequencing and single-cell transcriptomic analyses will elucidate the splicing shifts, while functional rescue via splice-switching oligonucleotides (SSOs) will ascertain the causal effect on DNA repair fidelity and tumor progression.
Abstract: We propose that in liver neoplasms, an elevation of GEMIN5, in concert with deregulated lncRNAs and other splicing modulators, directly alters the splicing of critical DNA repair transcripts—specifically RAD51 and MRE11. This direct modulation generates aberrant, noncanonical isoforms that impair high-fidelity homologous recombination, thereby favoring an error-prone break-induced replication (BIR) repair pathway. The shift in repair mechanism accelerates genomic instability which, in turn, fuels metastasis and angiogenesis characteristic of advanced liver cancers. To rigorously test this causal model, we will apply CRISPR/Cas9-mediated gene editing, enhanced CLIP-seq to confirm direct RNA binding, high-throughput isoform-specific RNA sequencing, and single-cell transcriptomics. In addition, functional rescue experiments using splice-switching oligonucleotides (SSOs) will be used to re-establish canonical splicing patterns, linking molecular changes with aggressive tumor phenotypes and poorer clinical prognosis. This integrated strategy leverages current technological capabilities to dissect the novel mechanism of splicing regulation by GEMIN5 in liver cancer.
CausalChain: GEMIN5 upregulation -> Direct binding to RAD51/MRE11 pre-mRNAs (validated by CLIP-seq) -> Aberrant alternative splicing producing noncanonical isoforms -> Shift from homologous recombination to error-prone BIR -> Increased genomic instability (measured by DNA damage markers) -> Enhanced metastasis/angiogenesis (observed in vitro and in vivo) -> Poorer liver neoplasm prognosis
